title: Acknowledgements
text: The data in this project was not generated by a machine. Every record began as a handwritten entry on a paper card, made by someone standing at a potting bench, often with soil on their hands. This page recognizes the people whose daily work created the archive that made this project possible.

title: Acknowledgements
text:
UBCBG Nursery propagation staff
The propagation cards span roughly fifty years of horticultural practice at the University of British Columbia Botanical Garden Nursery. Over that time, approximately twenty horticulturists, propagators, and nursery staff recorded their work on these cards. Their handwriting is, quite literally, the raw material of this project.

To be populated with individual acknowledgements as records are reviewed and staff identified. Many contributors can be recognized through initials and handwriting on the cards themselves.

title: Acknowledgements
text:
UBC Botanical Garden
This work exists within the broader institutional context of the UBC Botanical Garden, whose staff, administration, and volunteers, past and present, have maintained the living collections for over a century. The Garden’s commitment to conservation, research, and public education provides the foundation on which projects like this one are built.

PyMuPDF – PDF rendering and page extraction

Python and the broader scientific Python ecosystem

title: Use It
text: The tool is open source and designed to run on hardware you already own. You’ll need a machine that can run Ollama with a vision model, and your scanned cards as PDFs.

title: Use It
text:
Quick start
# 1. Clone
git clone https://github.com/Kkubeck/propagation-card-reader.git
cd propagation-card-reader

# 2. Conda env (Mac/Linux)
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate prop-card-reader

# 3. Start Ollama somewhere reachable and pull the vision model
ollama pull qwen2.5vl:7b

# 4. Build the RAG taxonomy index (one-time, from your accession CSV exports)
python rag_index_builder.py

# 5. Inventory PDFs, then process
python run.py inventory --pdf-dir path/to/cards
python run.py process --mode rag --dpi 175

# 6. Inspect / export
python db_viewer.py            # Streamlit UI
python run.py export -o out.csv

title: Use It
text:
What you need

A vision-capable LLM host — Ollama serving qwen2.5vl:7b. It can run on the same machine or another box on your network (point --ollama at it).
Your cards as PDFs — multi-page scans are fine; the tool splits them.
Accession exports (optional but recommended) — CSV exports from your collection system power the RAG taxonomy validation. The tool works without them, just with less cross-checking.

title: Use It
text:
CLI reference
run.py is the entry point:







Command
Purpose




inventory --pdf-dir DIR
Scan PDFs and build the card inventory


process --mode rag --dpi 175
Process pending cards through the pipeline


status
Show processing progress


export -o out.csv
Export extracted records to CSV


failures [--retry]
List or re-run failed cards



See the repository’s README.md and docs/ for full flags, the extraction schema, and card-layout field mappings.






Tip



This was built for one garden’s archive but is meant to generalize. If you’re at another institution with a paper propagation archive, the pipeline is the starting point — get in touch via the GitHub repo.

title: How It All Works
text: This page explains the technical concepts used by the Propagation Card Reader. Each concept is introduced through a concrete example from the project itself. No prior technical knowledge is assumed.

title: How It All Works
text:
The Basics

What is a model?
In this context, a “model” is a piece of software that has learned patterns from examples. Think of it like a new staff member who has read millions of documents on their first day. They have never seen your specific documents, in this case decades of propagation cards, but they have a general sense of what handwriting looks like, what dates look like, and even what Latin species names might look like.
When you show the model a card image, it draws on that general knowledge to produce a transcription. It is not following a set of rules someone wrote (“if you see ink marks in the top-left corner, that is the species name”). It is recognizing patterns it has seen before in other contexts and applying them to something new.


What are prompts and context?
Before the model attempts to read a card, it receives a prompt. This is a set of specific instructions that guides its focus. Instead of just asking “what does this say?”, the prompt injects expected information, essentially telling the model: “You are looking at a botanical record; expect to find a taxon name and an accession number. What does this say?”
This allows the model to leverage context. Traditional OCR (optical character recognition) looks at characters in isolation: a shape is either a “C” or a “G.” A Vision Language Model (VLM) looks at the entire image and surrounding words. If an ink smudge makes a letter ambiguous, but the surrounding letters are “O T O N E A S T E R”, the VLM uses its understanding of botanical sublanguage to definitively read Cotoneaster. It uses context to read the card more like a person would.

title: How It All Works
text:
The Hardware Reality

What do “local”, “tokens”, and “RAM” mean?
When we say the model runs “locally,” we mean it runs entirely on the physical computer sitting in front of you—perhaps a repurposed desktop node acting as the system’s brain. The card images are never uploaded to the internet.
This is the opposite of a cloud service, where data is sent to a massive enterprise data center. Cloud models are incredibly fast, but they charge you per token (the fundamental chunks of words a model reads and generates). When running locally, your token cost is zero; you only pay the amortized cost of the hardware and the electricity required to run it.
For a botanical garden, local processing ensures sensitive collection records such as rare species coordinates or donor names remain private. But it comes with a physical limit: RAM (Random Access Memory).
Enterprise cloud models expand across vast arrays of memory. A local machine has a fixed amount of unified memory. To work locally, the entire model must fit inside your machine’s RAM all at once. This requires us to use highly efficient models rather than the massive, resource-heavy versions used by big tech companies.


The DPI Trade-off
DPI stands for dots per inch, measuring how detailed a scanned image is. A higher DPI means more detail, which usually helps the model read finer handwriting.
However, because of the RAM limits on ‘local’ machines there is a strict trade-off. An image scanned at a high DPI creates a much larger file that takes up significant space in the machine’s unified memory. The larger the image footprint, the smaller the model we are forced to use to avoid running out of RAM.
The project settled on 150-175 DPI as the sweet spot: it provides enough detail to accurately read the handwriting while leaving enough memory free for a sufficiently smart model to do the heavy lifting.

(Placeholder: side-by-side comparison of the same card at 100, 150, and 200 DPI, showing the legibility difference.)

title: How It All Works
text:
The Software Reality

What are “open weights”?
The model used in this project (Qwen 2.5-VL) is described as “open-weight.” This means that the learned parameters, those are the patterns the model extracted from its training data, are freely available for anyone to download and use. You do not need to pay a subscription, sign a license agreement, or use a specific company’s platform.
This open nature is what makes the foundation of the tool portable. If another botanical garden wants to read their own cards, they can download the same model and run it on their own hardware.
However, it is not entirely “plug and play.” Because the system relies heavily on context, another institution would need to do two things to make it work for their records: 1. Personalize the prompts: The instructions must be adjusted to understand the specific layout and sublanguage of their garden’s cards as the current tool is highly tuned to UBCBG’s format. 2. Provide local data: They must supply their own internal collection reports. Specifically the database mapping their accession numbers to taxon names. This powers the Retrieval-Augmented Validation step.

title: How It All Works
text:
The Processing Logic

How does the model make a decision? (Decision Space & Temperature)
Under the hood, a model doesn’t “read” in the human sense; it calculates mathematical probabilities. For every token it generates, it assigns a probability score to what the next token should be. The range of all possible valid interpretations it considers is its decision space.
We can influence this math using a setting called temperature. A low temperature forces the model to be strict, always picking the single most mathematically probable token. A slightly higher temperature allows it to explore other highly probable paths within the decision space.
This is why a faded, ambiguous card might fail on the first attempt, but succeed on the second. By running the same card multiple times, we sample different paths through the decision space. While there are diminishing returns, eventually the model has exhausted its best guesses during repeated attempts, tending to mathematically converge on the correct answer.

(Placeholder: visualization showing answer space convergence across retries for a sample set of cards. A chart showing how the distribution of outputs narrows with repeated attempts.)



What is RAG and Retrieval-Augmented Validation?
RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation. In plain terms, it means giving the model a reference sheet to check its work against.
In this project, because the Garden already has a database of every known accession number and recorded species name in its history, we can inject this data into the process. We use a specific technique called Retrieval-Augmented Validation (RAV). When the model reads “Acer macrophyllum,” the system instantly checks that reading against the internal database. If it exists, confidence goes up. If the model reads “Acer macrophylllm” (three L’s), the system catches the likely typo and flags it.


What is post-processing?
The model reads, but the code checks. Post-processing is the secondary layer of code that takes the model’s raw transcription and standardizes it strictly to the Nursery’s sublanguage. It formats the dates, extracts the verified accession numbers, and filters out noise (like geographic coordinates or source codes that might look like accession numbers but aren’t).
Splitting the model’s probabilistic “guessing” from the code’s rigid “checking” is a crucial design decision. It lets each part focus on what it does best.

These concepts are not unique to propagation cards. The same ideas apply to any institution sitting on paper records: herbarium sheets, field notebooks, accession ledgers, library archives. The technology is general. The application here is specific, but the principles transfer.

Next: Results, what the pipeline actually produced.

title: The Cards
text: Before explaining how a computer reads a propagation card, it helps to understand what a propagation card actually is, what information it holds, and why the format is the way it is.

title: The Cards
text:
What you are looking at
A propagation card is a small paper record, measuring 8 inches wide by 5 inches tall, that tracks a single propagation event: one batch of seed sown, or one set of cuttings stuck. The card is created when material arrives and is updated by hand as the process unfolds.
Each card records:

The identity. The scientific name (genus, species, author), botanical family, and, in most cases, an accession number.
Where the material came from. A collector’s name, a collection number, a source institution, or a wild-collection site. Cards might also include extra information for the curator, such as flower color or a form particularity.
What was done to it. Sowing date, treatment(s) (cold stratification, soaking, scarification, etc.), growing medium, and location in the nursery.
What happened. Germination date, number of seedlings, transplant date, or failure and disposal.

The card is a complete biography of a propagation attempt, from arrival to its ultimate outcome: being planted out in the Botanical Garden.

Placeholder: annotated image of a dummy propagation card, showing each field labeled. Kevin to create sample cards that are safe for public display.

title: The Cards
text:
Two eras of card
The archive this project looked at spans roughly fifty years, and the card format changed partway through. Understanding the difference matters because the computer has to handle both.

Old cards (pre-2017)
The older cards are carbon-copy triplicates, written in pen or pencil. They have about seven rows of printed metadata fields across the top, with handwritten entries filled in. Dates are written as day/month/year. While the accession number format changed twice over five decades, it always maintained a clearly defined field on the right-hand side of the card.
These cards are often faded. The carbon copies, especially the second and third sheets, can be difficult to read even by eye.

Placeholder: image of a dummy old-format card.



New cards (post-2017)
When the garden adopted a new accession management system (IrisBG), the card format was simplified. New cards are printed on card stock with four rows of metadata. Dates are written as year/month/day.
This new format is not inherently “better” or cleaner than the old cards. The simplified layout simply reflects a diminished need to reproduce all the metadata on the physical card, since that information now exists in the digital Collection database. The legibility of these cards still varies entirely based on the handwriting of whoever filled them out.

Placeholder: image of a dummy new-format card.

title: The Cards
text:
The hard cases
Most cards follow a straightforward layout: one species, one sowing, a few dates, an outcome. But a significant portion of the archive contains cards that are harder to read, both for humans and machines.

Faded carbon copies
The oldest cards in the archive are carbon triplicates. The top copy is usually readable; the second and third copies can be ghostly. A person squinting at the card might recognize a familiar species name or fill in a date from context. Teaching a computer to do the same is a real challenge.


Condensed propagation tables
As cards piled up over the decades, workers took to condensing information. A propagator would use a single card to create a handwritten propagation table, recording a series of sowings of the same species across different years to allow for rapid comparison of techniques on identical taxa. These multi-sowing cards can contain five, ten, even fifteen separate accessions with their own dates and outcomes, packed into a space designed for a single observation.
These are among the most valuable records in the archive because they show repeated attempts with the same species over time. They are also the hardest for the computer to parse correctly.


Duplexed cards (Two-sided records)
When space ran out on the front of a card, propagators simply flipped it over. Important notes, secondary treatments, continued observations, and expanded propagation tables were frequently written on the back. A system reading these records must be able to link the front and back scans of the same physical card to process it as a single logical document.


No accession number
Before roughly 2012, a propagation attempt did not receive an accession number until it succeeded. If a sowing failed, the card was filed with no accession at all, only a species name.
This means that for the earliest decades of the archive, failed attempts are essentially invisible to the accession database. The card may be the only surviving record that the attempt was ever made. Reading these cards recovers information that otherwise would not exist in any digital system.

title: The Cards
text:
Why the cards matter
It is easy to look at a filing cabinet full of handwritten cards and see a data entry problem. But that framing misses the point.
These cards represent institutional memory: the accumulated judgment of every propagator who worked at the garden. Which species need cold stratification. How long to soak a hard-coated seed. Which treatments were tried and failed. When to give up and when to wait another season.
That knowledge is not in any textbook. It was learned by doing, recorded by hand, and filed away. When the person who wrote the card retires, the knowledge does not transfer automatically. It sits in the drawer, waiting for someone to ask the right question.
Beyond capturing techniques, there is the profound possibility of recapturing data that has been “lost” to the current system due to decades of historical data management shifts. There are mature plants growing in the Garden right now whose early histories were severed from their digital records during past database migrations. By digitizing the original paper, we have the promising potential to give these “silent” accessions a voice again, re-rooting them in their own documented history. While we haven’t yet analyzed the resulting database closely enough to find specific examples, the prospect of reconnecting a living collection with its forgotten origins remains one of the most exciting possibilities of this work.
The purpose of this project is to make it possible to ask those questions and recover those stories.

Next: The Journey, the story of three attempts to teach a computer to read these cards.

title: Propagation Card Reader
text:
For more than fifty years, the people who grow plants for a botanical garden have been recording their processes on small paper cards. Every seed sown, every cutting stuck, every success and failure, written by hand and filed in a cabinet.
Thousands of cards. Decades of knowledge. Sitting in drawers.
This project reads them.

title: Propagation Card Reader
text:
What are propagation cards?
Every plant production facility needs to document its processes, if only to make things more efficient the next time around. This documentation becomes critical when the “next time” is twenty years from now, and a completely different person is doing the work. At the UBCBG Nursery, we handle diverse and sometimes rare material that might never be collected again. Maximizing the probability of success is imperative.
Historically, before digital databases, the “accession card” was the primary record of a plant’s existence in the Collection. These were printed in triplicate: the top copy accompanied the seed packet to the nursery, while the other two remained with the Collection Technician and the Curator. Because of this historical workflow, the terms “accession card” and “propagation card” are used interchangeably in this project.
The card follows that material through every physical step at the Nursery: sowing, treatment, germination, transplanting. The original intent was that each card act as a single observation of a single accession, handwritten by the person doing the work. Over the decades, as cards piled up, workers took to condensing the information. They created hand-written propagation tables on the cards to allow for rapid comparison of techniques on identical taxa. Older physical cards whose data was considered ‘captured’ were often reused as scrap, preserving only the most critical propagation outcomes.
Today, while modern propagation data was eventually digitized (utilizing IrisBG since 2017), it is rarely entered directly into a computer on the spot. The Nursery is a messy, dusty environment where physical cards and pen annotations remain far more practical than screens. Furthermore, writing on the cards first provides a crucial audit trail. It allows multiple staff members to execute the physical work at the potting bench while centralizing the final database entry to maintain strict data hygiene. Even with modern systems in place, horticulturists reference these older paper cards when developing protocols to see what has worked in the past, and just as importantly, what hasn’t.
Over time, these cards accumulate into something extraordinary: a complete record of what an institution has tried. They hold the craft knowledge of generations of horticulturists.






The quiet crisis. When experienced propagation staff retire, their knowledge often leaves with them. The cards remain, but without context they become harder and harder to interpret. Eventually, someone decides they’re taking up space. Or a natural disaster removes the choice altogether.

title: Propagation Card Reader
text:
What this project does
The Propagation Card Reader is a tool that takes scanned images of handwritten propagation cards and extracts structured data from them: species names, dates, treatments, outcomes, accession numbers. It turns paper into a searchable database.
It does this using a vision language model, a type of software that can look at an image and describe what it sees, similar to how a person would read the card. The model runs entirely on a single laptop. No cloud service, no subscription, no per-page fee. The card images never leave the building.

title: Propagation Card Reader
text:
Why this site exists
This is not just documentation for a piece of software. It is an attempt to explain, accessibly, the ideas behind the technology, and to tell the story of how it came together.
If you work at a botanical garden and have never touched a line of code, start with The Cards. You will recognize what you see.
If you are curious about how a computer reads handwriting, The Journey walks through three attempts to solve that problem, each one teaching something new.
If you want to understand the technical concepts without a computer science degree, How It All Works explains things like “language model” and “decision space” using the cards as examples.
If you want the numbers, go to Results. If you want to run it yourself, go to Use It. And if you want to know who made this possible, see the Acknowledgements.

Every botanical garden has knowledge locked in paper. Herbarium sheets, field notebooks, accession ledgers, propagation cards. The methods described here are not limited to one type of record or one institution. A laptop, a scanner, and an open-weight model: that is all it takes.
See the code on GitHub

title: The Journey
text:
This project did not start with the solution it uses today. It went through three distinct attempts, each one a response to the limitations of the technology available at the time and a reflection of a steep personal learning curve.
It would be inaccurate to view these methods as competing options; rather, they represent an evolution over time. When this work began, a site-specific custom pipeline was the only programmatic alternative to manually typing out data from all 12,000 cards one by one. Each subsequent iteration benefited from rapid advancements in machine learning frameworks and an increasing familiarity with modern coding tools.

title: The Journey
section: Attempt 1: Building a custom pipeline from scratch
text:
Attempt 1: Building a custom pipeline from scratch
The first idea was the most intuitive one. If a computer needs to read specific handwriting on specific forms, you build and train a system from scratch to do exactly that.
Using classic data science libraries like scikit-learn and deep learning frameworks like PyTorch, this approach required manually segmenting images and painstakingly labeling training data character by character, line by line. The goal was to feed thousands of exact examples into a custom architecture so it could learn to map images of text to the actual characters they represented.
The bottleneck here was variation paired with the sheer scale of manual labor required for a single person working in their spare time. The archive spans over fifty years and contains the handwriting of dozens of different staff members. Some entries are in typewriter text, others in crisp pen, still others are written in faint pencil, and a few are ghostly carbon copies.
To make a custom PyTorch model robust enough to handle this level of noise, it required an impractical amount of manually labeled training data. Without it, the model simply could not generalize across different eras and handwriting styles.






What this taught me. Custom training works beautifully when data is completely uniform. When data is historical, messy, and varied, you waste months labeling data just to get a model to recognize basic shapes. To avoid this, you need a model that already arrives with a general understanding of what writing looks like.

title: The Journey
section: Attempt 2: OpenCV alignment and Google Cloud Vision
text:
Attempt 2: OpenCV alignment and Google Cloud Vision
The second approach split the problem in two: use computer vision to find things on the card, and use a commercial cloud service to read them.
The first half worked beautifully. Using OpenCV, a widely used open-source computer vision library, I built an image alignment module that could reliably locate the card within a scanned page. A multi-template matching approach tried several anchor variations to find the best alignment, achieving 100% success on card detection.
The plan was to combine this geometric alignment with fixed-coordinate templates: if the card is aligned, then the species name is always at these pixel coordinates, the accession number is always at those coordinates, and so on. But propagation cards are not standardized forms. Propagators wrote outside boxes, used margins for notes, and the internal layout shifted across decades. Fixed coordinates broke immediately.
The pivot was to use Google Cloud Vision for the reading itself. Google’s API returned both the recognized text and the pixel coordinates of each word on the page. Custom code then mapped those word positions back to structured fields based on proximity to known field labels: a form of dynamic template matching that adapted to wherever the text actually appeared.
This strategy yielded highly readable text outputs. The cloud engine handled handwriting variations with ease because it was built upon the exact deep-learning principles experimented with in Attempt 1, but scaled across billions of data points. On the fields it targeted, the approach reached roughly 90 to 98 percent accuracy.
However, the approach was ultimately abandoned due to institutional reality. Processing thousands of records would have meant sending sensitive institutional collection data, including wild-collection provenance and donor details, to external corporate servers. It became clear that navigating data sovereignty and securing institutional approval for off-site processing was a massive hurdle. Furthermore, template matching, even the dynamic version, proved exceptionally brittle. The moment a horticulturist built a condensed propagation table or reused the back of a card for a different species, the spatial logic broke entirely.






What this taught me. General-purpose models solve the handwriting barrier, but cloud dependencies introduce issues with data sovereignty, subscription fees, and corporate reliance. For an institution prioritizing data privacy and long-term autonomy, cloud-only pipelines are frequently a non-starter.

title: The Journey
text:
Attempt 3: Local vision language models
The current iteration of this project is cutting-edge, utilizing tools and architectures that did not exist even a year ago. The convergence of open-weight vision models, local execution engines like Ollama, local computing nodes, and advanced agentic development tools over the past 12 months has fundamentally changed what is possible on ordinary hardware. I say this not as a boast but as a call to regular folks like myself: these techniques are now available to the masses.
Instead of traditional OCR that looks at characters in isolation, a Vision Language Model (VLM) views the entire image holistically. It reads a propagation card much like a human archivist would: interpreting terms from context, parsing layout structure naturally, and outputting clean text.

Finding the right model
The development of this pipeline began on a small desktop node running Gemma 3, Google’s open-weight model, served locally through Ollama. Gemma handled general text well, but its accuracy on the specific challenges of propagation cards, faded handwriting, botanical Latin, and condensed tables, was not sufficient for production use.
When the pipeline moved to a MacBook for deployment, Qwen 2.5-VL had just been released by Alibaba’s research team. The Qwen family offered vision-language models at several sizes, and initial testing showed markedly better performance on handwritten botanical records.
The question became which size to use. Larger models (12B and 14B parameters) produced slightly better transcriptions, but combining their memory footprint with the high-DPI scans required to read faded writing quickly overwhelmed the machine’s 24 GB of unified RAM. The model and the image compete for the same memory: a larger model means less room for a detailed scan, and vice versa.
Qwen 2.5-VL at 7 billion parameters, paired with 175 DPI scans, struck the balance. The model was sharp enough to read decades of varied handwriting, and the scan resolution was high enough to preserve faded characters, all within the memory budget of a single laptop. This is the configuration that processed the full archive.
It is worth noting that there is no strict adherence to this specific model. Other botanical gardens adapting this tool should absolutely experiment with newer, larger models if they have the hardware to support them. I designed this as a “one and done” solution; the results are good enough that I expect never to have to run this archive again.


The virtue of patience
Running a multi-billion-parameter neural network locally on a desktop or a repurposed hardware node changes the performance dynamic. It is slower than a massive cloud data center.
However, as horticulturists, we are intimately familiar with waiting. When you sow a seed, you don’t expect results overnight; we understand that complex systems take time to yield results. Local machine learning requires a similar mindset. The trade-off for absolute data sovereignty and zero operational cost is processing time. We are perfectly comfortable letting a local machine quietly run through the night, germinating structured data from cold pixels at its own steady pace.


Splitting the labor
To maximize accuracy on local hardware, the codebase splits the work into a two-part pipeline:

The model reads. The VLM is instructed strictly to transcribe everything it sees as a faithful observer. It is not asked to format or interpret data during the vision pass, which preserves its full cognitive capacity for raw comprehension.
The code checks. A robust post-processing layer handles the rigid logic: formatting dates, isolating accession strings, and executing Retrieval-Augmented Validation (RAV) against internal collection reports to catch spelling errors or typos.







What this taught me. You do not need to build your own AI from scratch, nor do you need to pay for massive cloud infrastructure. A compact, open-weight model running locally can handle historical records beautifully if you divide the labor. Let the model do the probabilistic reading and let deterministic local code handle the structural verification.

title: Results
text:
RAG-assisted extraction
92% of cards (11,524) received taxonomy hints from the RAG index during extraction, averaging 458 tokens of context per card with a retrieval latency of 14 ms. The RAG step provides the model with accession-to-taxon mappings from the institution’s database, improving accession number and botanical name accuracy without additional model calls.

title: Results
text:
Accuracy
Field-level accuracy scoring against a manually reviewed sample has not yet been completed. The earlier prototype (OpenCV alignment + Google Cloud Vision with dynamic template matching) reached roughly 90-98% accuracy on the fields it targeted, useful as a reference point, though it required cloud calls, an internet connection, and far narrower scope.
A formal accuracy assessment is planned: a stratified sample of cards (old vs. new, seed vs. cutting, single vs. multi-sowing) scored against ground-truth transcriptions.

title: Results
text:
Honest failure modes
Credibility comes from naming what doesn’t work:

Condensed multi-sowing tables: the hardest case. Several accessions on one card in a hand-drawn table format. Easy to merge or drop rows. These represent approximately 17% of cards with unknown extraction outcomes.
Faded carbon copies: low-contrast old cards (pre-1980s triplicates) degrade transcription quality.
Ambiguous handwriting on accession digits: a single misread digit produces a plausible-but-wrong accession. The RAG validation step catches many of these, but not all.
No-accession cards: pre-2012 failed sowings rely on taxon-name matching, which inherits any error in the taxon transcription.
Family name case inconsistency: the model transcribes family names as written on the card, producing duplicates like “Ericaceae” and “ERICACEAE.” Normalizable in post-processing, but present in the raw output.

title: About
text:
Propagation Card Reader began as a practical problem at the UBC Botanical Garden Nursery: there were decades of handwritten propagation cards holding hard-won horticultural knowledge—such as sowing dates, treatments, successes, and failures—but no realistic way to digitize them. Commercial OCR meant ongoing cloud costs and sending collection data off-site, while manual entry required staff time the Garden simply didn’t have.
The answer was to run a vision-language model locally. It is free, private, and adept enough at parsing messy handwriting to be genuinely useful. This approach was highly effective because the knowledge on the cards utilizes a relatively restricted sublanguage, and portions of the expected OCR output—specifically accession numbers and taxon name associations—are already known and predictable.

title: About
text:
The author
Built by Kevin Kubeck, a horticulturist at UBC Botanical Garden with decades of propagation and plant-collection experience, alongside a self-taught background in Python, data science, and data tooling for conservation.
The first two versions of this project were built independently. This final iteration utilized an agentic coding workflow, leveraging Claude Opus 4.6 as an orchestrator and the local openclaw system as a harness.

title: About
text:
Why local-first matters
For a botanical garden, collection data can be highly sensitive, especially when it involves rare-species locations, provenance, and historical institutional records. Keeping the entire OCR pipeline on local hardware ensures the garden never has to trade privacy or budget for the benefits of digitization. That principle is the core motivation behind this tool.
